nameStory: The striped maple earned its name from the distinctive white stripes that run vertically along its smooth, green bark, creating a zebra-like pattern that's unmistakable in the forest. It's also called 'moosewood' because moose love to browse on its tender bark and twigs, especially in winter when other food is scarce. The name 'whistlewood' comes from the fact that you can easily slip the bark off young twigs to make simple whistles.
description: Striped maple is a small understory tree that rarely grows taller than 20-30 feet, looking more like a large shrub in many forest settings. It's one of our most shade-loving maples, thriving in the dim light beneath the forest canopy where other trees struggle. The tree has a distinctly tropical look with its large, broad leaves and smooth, striped bark that makes it stand out among New England's typically rough-barked trees. It grows slowly and often has multiple trunks, creating a graceful, open branching pattern.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth, bright green bark with prominent white vertical stripes running up the trunk like racing stripes on a car. The bark feels cool and smooth to the touch, almost like skin, and the stripes are raised slightly so you can feel them with your fingertips.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, broad leaves shaped like a goose's foot with three main lobes and smaller side lobes. They're much bigger than most maple leaves (4-8 inches long) and have a soft, almost velvety feel underneath with prominent veins you can trace with your finger.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Small, slender tree or large shrub that often grows with multiple trunks from the base. Branches are thin and flexible, often drooping gracefully, and the overall shape is open and airy rather than dense.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, greenish-yellow flowers hang in drooping clusters like tiny bells in late spring. Individual flowers are small but the drooping clusters (called racemes) are 3-6 inches long and quite noticeable against the bright green bark.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Typical maple 'helicopter' seeds (samaras) but smaller than sugar maple seeds, with wings that form a wide V-shape. They're often pinkish or reddish when young, maturing to brown in late summer.

habitat: Striped maple thrives in the cool, moist understory of mature hardwood and mixed forests throughout New England's mountains and hills. You'll find it growing in the dappled shade beneath sugar maples, beech, and birch trees, often on north-facing slopes or in ravines where the soil stays consistently moist. It's particularly common in the higher elevations of the White Mountains, Green Mountains, and Berkshires, but can be found in suitable forest habitats down to sea level.

seasonality.spring: Long clusters of small, bell-like flowers appear in May, hanging gracefully from the branches just as the large leaves are unfurling. The contrast between the drooping yellow-green flower clusters and the bright striped bark is particularly striking.
seasonality.summer: The large, soft leaves provide excellent shade identification opportunities, and the smooth green bark with white stripes is at its most vibrant. Young winged seeds develop and are often tinged with pink or red.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn bright yellow to orange, sometimes with red tinges, creating a warm glow in the understory. The large leaves are among the first to fall, often carpeting the forest floor by early October.
seasonality.winter: The striped bark becomes the main identification feature, standing out dramatically against snow. Young twigs are bright green and flexible, and the graceful branching pattern is clearly visible without leaves.

funFact: Striped maple is a 'sequential hermaphrodite' that can actually change its sex from year to year depending on environmental conditions - a young tree might produce male flowers, then switch to female flowers when it gets bigger and has more energy, and even switch back to male during stressful years!
confusionNotes: The only tree you might confuse striped maple with is mountain maple, but mountain maple has rough, grayish bark without stripes and much smaller leaves with more pointed lobes. Remember: if you see those distinctive white stripes on green bark, you've found your striped maple - no other tree in New England has this feature.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'moosewood,' this tree is also browsed heavily by deer, and in some areas, overbrowsing by deer is making it less common in the understory. It's the only North American representative of the 'snakebark maples,' a group that includes several Asian species with similar striped bark patterns.
compareHints: Unlike its maple relatives, striped maple has the distinctive white-striped bark that no other North American maple possesses. While mountain maple is also a small understory species, it lacks the stripes and has smaller, more deeply lobed leaves. The large, soft leaves of striped maple are also much bigger and broader than those of red maple or sugar maple, giving it an almost tropical appearance that's unique among New England maples.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red maple differs from sugar maple by its toothed leaf margins, red leaf stems, and earlier seed drop.
Among New England's maples, sugar maples have the smoothest leaf edges (no teeth) and the most rounded lobe shapes, while red maples have serrated edges and more pointed lobes.
Norway maple differs from sugar maple by its milky leaf sap, earlier and more chartreuse spring flowers, and wider-angled seed wings.
Box elder stands out dramatically from other New England maples because it's the only one with compound leaves instead of the classic lobed maple leaf shape.
Among New England's maples, mountain maple is the odd one out—it's the only one that stays truly shrubby and forms colonies rather than growing into a single-trunked tree.

Among New England maples, silver maple stands out for its deeply dissected leaves and silvery undersides - much more dramatic than the shallow lobes of red maple or the more rounded lobes of sugar maple.
Among New England maples, sycamore maple stands out for its exceptionally large leaves on long stalks and drooping flower clusters.
Among New England maples, Amur maple is unique for its consistently small size and three-lobed leaves with the distinctly elongated center lobe.

Japanese maple differs from all native New England maples by having much more deeply divided, delicate leaves with 5-9 narrow lobes compared to the broader, less-divided leaves of sugar maple, red maple, and silver maple.
Field maple is much smaller than sugar maple, red maple, or Norway maple, with distinctively small, thick, round-lobed leaves that set it apart from all other maples in New England.
